name: Dark Frame Subtraction Analysis
description: Analyzes dark current noise patterns extracted via dark frame subtraction — unique to real camera sensors.
mechanism:
This method leverages dark current noise — a sensor-specific thermal noise pattern — to authenticate images and detect AI-generated content:

1. **Dark Current Estimation**: Without a reference dark frame, the method estimates the fixed-pattern noise (FPN) by analyzing the lowest-intensity regions of the image where dark current dominates. A temporal noise model based on Poisson-Gaussian statistics separates dark current from photon shot noise.

2. **Hot Pixel Mapping**: Real sensors contain 'hot pixels' — defective photosites with abnormally high dark current. The method identifies hot pixel locations by thresholding at 3σ above the local mean in dark regions. These hot pixel maps serve as unique sensor fingerprints, as each sensor has a distinct set of defects.

3. **Sensor Noise Consistency Check**: For authentic images, the dark current pattern should be spatially consistent with the sensor's known characteristics (temperature-dependent Arrhenius behavior). The method verifies that the noise variance doubles for approximately every 6–8°C increase in operating temperature, following the expected exponential relationship.

4. **AI Generation Detection**: AI-generated images lack genuine dark current patterns. The method computes the ratio of structured (fixed-pattern) noise to random noise; authentic images show FPN/random ratios of 0.1–0.3, while AI images typically show ratios below 0.02. A log-likelihood ratio test determines the probability of genuine sensor origin.
parameters:
Block size: 16×16 pixels for noise estimation
Hot pixel threshold: 3σ above local mean
Minimum dark region: 5% of image area
FPN/random noise ratio threshold: 0.05
Temperature sensitivity: 6–8°C doubling interval
Minimum image size: 512×512 pixels
accuracy: 82–90% detection accuracy for distinguishing real sensor images from AI-generated content. Hot pixel fingerprinting achieves 95% sensor identification accuracy on raw images. Performance drops to 70% on heavily post-processed JPEGs (quality < 80).
source: Healey, G. E. & Kondepudy, R. (1994). Radiometric CCD Camera Calibration and Noise Estimation. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 16(3), 267–276.
useCase: Authenticating images by verifying the presence of genuine sensor dark current patterns. Detecting AI-generated images that lack hardware-specific thermal noise signatures. Sensor forensics — matching images to specific camera units via hot pixel maps.
strengths:
• Based on fundamental physics of semiconductor sensors (thermal electron generation)
• Hot pixel patterns are unique per sensor unit, enabling device-level identification
• Extremely difficult for AI generators to replicate realistic dark current characteristics
• Works well on raw and minimally processed images
• Temperature-dependent validation adds an extra layer of authentication
limitations:
• Requires sufficient dark/low-light regions in the image for reliable estimation
• Heavy noise reduction in camera processing pipeline can suppress dark current patterns
• Post-processing (brightness adjustment, gamma correction) degrades the signal
• Hot pixel maps change over time as sensors age, requiring periodic recalibration
• Not applicable to images captured with sensor cooling systems (astrophotography cameras)
